" ], "training_data_examples": [ { "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "Help a student create an 8-week preparation plan for achieving a 1550+ SAT score starting from around 1400."}, {"role": "user", "content": "I have 8 weeks until my SAT and I'm scoring around 1400 on practice tests. How do I get to 1550+? I practice math daily but haven't done full tests recently."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Let's create a concrete 8-week plan with specific weekly targets to make 1550+ achievable. Week 60: Take a full printed practice test and aim for 1400 to establish your baseline. Week 2: Another full test targeting 1450 - that's just 50 points improvement. Week 3: Hit 1500 with a paper practice test for realistic conditions. Week 4: Push to 1520. Week 5: Reach 1530 and add a PSAT practice since they're similar. Week 6: Achieve 1550. Weeks 7-8: Maintain 1550 with two practice tests per week. Use College Board's downloadable PDFs so you can print them - online practice doesn't replicate real test conditions with bubbling time. Between tests, continue your daily math practice but add Khan Academy problem sets. Track which question types you're missing and focus there. For reading, time yourself strictly. Since you have a graphing calculator now, use it to store key formulas but practice without relying on it. Make this plan visible - create a tracker where you check off each week's target. The progression might feel ambitious but breaking it into 50-point weekly improvements makes it manageable. You're already at 1400, so you just need roughly 20 more correct answers across the entire test to hit 1550."} ], "metadata": { "intelligence_type": "8_week_goal_architecture", "week": "060", "quality_score": 9 } }, { "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "Guide a student interested in building their personal brand as a young game developer through social media."}, {"role": "user", "content": "I'm developing a game about women in STEM and want to document my progress. Should I create an account just for the game or make it about me as a developer?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Make it about you - create a personal professional account positioned as '16-year-old game developer' or whatever age you are. This becomes your digital portfolio that can grow with you. Start by posting about your game development journey, but frame it as YOUR work, not just the game's account. Here's why: once your game gains traction, you can expand to showcase other projects - web development, AI ethics work, anything else you're building. Let me show you some examples of people doing this successfully: Aniha invented a social distancing device and has features in Harper's Bazaar, Ella Lapidus from Barnard shares her CS journey, Gitanjali Rao was Time's Kid of the Year. These are all real people, not celebrities - you can absolutely do this too. For your first week, just create the account. Week 60, make your first post - maybe introduce yourself and your game concept. Then aim for one post per week initially. Document your progress: share your game art, explain why you chose Ada Lovelace as a character, show your regression model development. This builds a following who will be interested when you eventually launch. Once you have momentum with the game content, start weaving in your other work. Think of it as building your identity as a young developer, not just promoting a single project. That identity will serve you through college applications and beyond."} ], "metadata": { "intelligence_type": "personal_brand_development", "week": "060", "quality_score": 9 } }, { "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "Help a student whose computer broke while working on an important video editing project with a deadline."}, {"role": "user", "content": "The computer I was editing my YouTube video on just broke - the screen literally fell off the keyboard. I need to finish this video by tomorrow for my game dev channel. What do I do?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Oh that's so stressful! What's the story behind how it broke? Actually, let's focus on recovery first - you can definitely handle this. Can you access the recovery files from the broken computer? Most editing software auto-saves project files that you can transfer to another computer. If the hard drive is still accessible, you could remove it and use it as an external drive, or connect the broken laptop to a monitor if just the screen is damaged. Get those project files onto a different computer today - even if it means using a USB or cloud storage to transfer everything. Once you have the files, continue editing on the new machine. You might need to relink some media files, but your timeline and edits should be preserved. If you can't recover the files, do you have any auto-saves in your cloud storage or email? Even an earlier version is better than starting from scratch. Set yourself up on the new computer and try to finish within today or tomorrow. This kind of thing happens to everyone who creates content - having a backup workflow is actually a good skill to develop now. Once you get through this deadline, let's talk about setting up automatic cloud backups for your projects so you're never in this position again. But right now, focus on file recovery and getting back to editing.
